candidates.teaser: This animal gets bitten by a cobra, passes out cold — then wakes up and keeps eating the snake.
candidates.video_title: This Animal Survives Cobra Bites Like Nothing
candidates.video_description: The honey badger is almost entirely immune to venom, including cobra and mamba bites. After losing consciousness, it simply wakes up and continues its meal. Scientists still don't fully understand how.
candidates.script: A cobra bites this animal directly in the face. It collapses. Looks dead. Then, two hours later, it stands up, shakes it off, and finishes eating the cobra. The honey badger has protein mutations in its nerve cells that block venom from binding — the same mutation that makes some humans resistant to certain poisons. It doesn't avoid venomous snakes. It hunts them on purpose. What other animal do you think could survive that?

candidates.teaser: A blue whale's heart is so large, a human could literally crawl through its arteries.
candidates.video_title: You Could Swim Inside a Blue Whale's Heart
candidates.video_description: The blue whale's heart weighs around 180 kilograms and its main arteries are wide enough for a child to crawl through. It beats only 2 times per minute when diving. It is the largest heart of any animal ever recorded.
candidates.script: A blue whale's heart is the size of a small car — roughly 180 kilograms. Its main artery is so wide a human child could physically crawl through it. When the whale dives deep, that heart slows to just 2 beats per minute to conserve oxygen. At the surface, it jumps back to 37. This single organ pumps 220 liters of blood with every beat. Earth's largest animal has always had the largest heart — but did it evolve that way, or did the ocean force it?

candidates.topic: The Eiffel Tower Grows in Summer
candidates.teaser: The Eiffel Tower is a completely different height in summer than in winter — and it's not a small difference.
candidates.video_title: The Eiffel Tower Changes Height Every Summer
candidates.video_description: Due to thermal expansion, the iron structure of the Eiffel Tower grows up to 15 centimeters taller in summer heat. The same principle affects bridges, railways, and skyscrapers worldwide. Engineers must account for this in every large metal structure.
candidates.script: The Eiffel Tower is shorter in winter than in summer — by up to 15 centimeters. Iron expands when heated, and the tower's 7,300 tons of metal respond to every degree of temperature change. On a hot Paris afternoon, the entire structure physically grows. This isn't a flaw — engineers knew. Every bridge, railway track, and skyscraper on Earth is designed around the same principle. So the landmark you photographed in July? You've never seen it at its true winter height.

candidates.topic: Clocks on GPS Satellites Run Faster
candidates.teaser: Without a correction Einstein predicted over a century ago, every GPS on Earth would be wrong by miles — every single day.
candidates.video_title: Einstein Keeps Your GPS Accurate Every Day
candidates.video_description: GPS satellites orbit Earth at high speed and lower gravity, causing their onboard clocks to run faster than clocks on the ground. Without relativistic corrections based on Einstein's equations, GPS systems would accumulate errors of up to 11 kilometers per day.
candidates.script: Your GPS is wrong right now — and Einstein's math is the only thing fixing it. Satellites orbit 20,000 kilometers above Earth where gravity is weaker, so their clocks tick faster than ours. Without a correction built into every GPS satellite, your location would drift by 11 kilometers every single day. This isn't a software patch. It's Einstein's theory of relativity, published in 1915, baked directly into navigation hardware. Your phone finds a coffee shop because a dead physicist did math no one believed.

candidates.teaser: They poisoned him, shot him, beat him, and drowned him — and he still nearly escaped.
candidates.video_title: The Man Who Refused to Die — Rasputin
candidates.video_description: In December 1916, Russian mystic Rasputin was poisoned with cyanide-laced food, shot multiple times, beaten, and thrown into a frozen river — yet he reportedly kept moving at several stages. The exact sequence of events remains disputed by historians and forensic experts.
candidates.script: In December 1916, a group of Russian nobles fed Rasputin enough cyanide to kill five men. He drank wine laced with it and ate the poisoned cakes. Nothing happened. So they shot him. He fell. Then he got up. They beat him and shot him again — three more times. Then they tied him up and threw him into a frozen river. The autopsy found water in his lungs. He was still alive when he hit the water. Was he simply impossible to kill, or was the whole story exaggerated to protect someone?
